evidence: Tac. Ann. 1.61: aggerēs ūmidō palūdum … impōnere (Lewis & Short)

terms.gloss: the raised bed of a road, a causeway
evidence: Verg. A. 5.273: viae dēprēnsus in aggere serpēns (Lewis & Short s.v. agger)
Tac. Hist. 2.24: aggerem viae trēs praetōriae cohortēs obtinuēre (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Agger is earth heaped up, a mound or rampart; with viae (Vergil and Tacitus) the built-up road itself. Lewis & Short notes that in this sense classical authors always add viae, and agger alone for a road is later Latin.
“A crossing on foot”; Lewis & Short has agger for a causeway through a swamp.

sources: John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, p. 288.
Lewis & Short: agger
Quotations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them, in the house spelling; they have not been checked against a modern edition.
